what_to_do: Add light in the early morning on a timer so the day totals 14 to 16 hours, and let them go to roost with the sunset.
Do not light adult birds for more than 16 hours a day (Penn State).
Keep at least 6 hours of unbroken dark.
One 4 to 5 watt LED (40 watt equivalent) per 100 sq ft is enough, about bright enough to read a newspaper.
Once you start a lighting program, keep it going. Cutting it back drops production.
Extra light gives more winter eggs, not more eggs over a hen's life (Merck).
name: Daylight needed to keep laying
summary: Hens need about 14 hours of light a day to lay steadily. Below about 12 hours, laying drops and often stops.

summary: Most hens lay well for 2 to 3 years and on and off for a few more. Hens commonly live about 3 to 8 years, and some reach 10 to 15.

Let hens molt fully in their second winter; Oregon State suggests turning extra lights off for about 6 weeks so the molt is complete.
conflict_notes: Merck: typically 3 to 4 months, sometimes longer. Penn State: about 10 to 12 weeks to finish and return to lay. Mississippi State: 2 to 3 months for late molters, up to 4 to 6 for early molters.
name: Molting season and length
summary: Most hens molt once a year, usually in autumn as days shorten. A molt usually takes about 2 to 4 months. Good layers (late molters) drop feathers fast and finish in 2 to 3 months. Poor layers (early molters) can take 4 to 6 months.
notes: With extra lighting, hens usually lay about a year before molting (Merck). Feathers drop in a set order: head, neck, breast, body, wings, then tail (Mississippi State).

name: Laying in year 1
summary: The best year. Production climbs quickly after the first egg and peaks at about 35 weeks, when a good flock lays more than 9 eggs per 10 hens a day. The peak lasts about 10 weeks, then slowly declines.
notes: Breed matters a lot. A commercial White Leghorn averages about 265 eggs a year, backyard breeds lay fewer, and some heritage breeds lay only 50 to 100 (Penn State).

summary: Still good, but fewer eggs than year 1. Eggs get bigger and shells get weaker each year. Most hens go through a full molt before or during their second laying season.

summary: The comb and wattles grow and turn bright red and waxy. She squats when you reach toward her. She starts sitting in and rearranging the nest boxes. These signs come from a few days to about 2 to 3 weeks before the first egg.

summary: A broody hen stops laying so she can sit on eggs, even when there are none. Left alone, she can stay broody for 3 to 4 weeks. Cochins and Silkies go broody often, Leghorns rarely.

summary: Hens drop and regrow their feathers, usually in autumn as days shorten. Energy goes into feathers, so laying stops until the molt is done.
